pronunciation.note: Kānāloa keeps the Hawaiian macrons that mark vowel length — a phonemic feature of the language, and one the ASCII form loses. The lexicon nevertheless classifies the name Tier 2: the macron marks quantity, and the name carries no distinctive non-Latin letter or mark such as the glottal ʻokina (which would have changed the consonants themselves). The rhythm of the long vowels is the name's dignity, but by the mechanical rule it stays Tier 2.

domains.title: Lord of the Vast Ocean
domains.subtitle: Sea, Underworld, and Healing
domains.lead: Kānāloa is the Hawaiian god of the deep ocean, the underworld, and healing. He is the companion and sometimes rival of Kāne, the creator; while Kāne governs fresh water and life, Kānāloa rules the salt sea and the mysteries beneath it. He is associated with the octopus, whose arms reach in all directions like ocean currents.

cards.name: Vast Ocean
cards.desc: The Pacific itself is his body, source of food, travel, and the unknown.

cards.name: Underworld
cards.desc: He receives the dead into the dark realm beneath land and sea.

cards.name: Healer
cards.desc: Kānāloa and Kāne together discovered medicinal plants and healing arts.

cards.name: Octopus Kin

mythology.lead: Hawaiian myths present Kānāloa as a complementary power to Kāne, the creator. Their partnership structures much of traditional cosmology: one god of fresh water and daylight, one of salt sea and depth, together covering the whole of the living world.

myths.title: Kāne and Kānāloa
myths.text: In Hawaiian cosmogony, Kāne and Kānāloa are paired creator gods. Beckwith's Hawaiian Mythology preserves the tradition that the two traveled together across the primordial ocean, striking the earth with their staffs to open springs of fresh water — Kāne's gift of life in the midst of Kānāloa's salt realm — and calling forth the plants and creatures of the islands. Kāne is the fresh water and the sunlight; Kānāloa is the salt sea that surrounds and sustains the land. Their partnership is not hierarchy but dynamic balance: no island exists without both the spring and the surrounding ocean, and the two gods are invoked together so often that the pairing itself became a formula of blessing. The myth encodes an ecological truth the Hawaiians lived by — life on an island is a negotiation between land and sea, and neither partner can be dispensed with.

myths.title: The Discovery of Medicine
myths.text: The healing tradition, recorded by Kamakau and Malo, begins with Kānāloa himself falling ill, and no remedy in the world able to help him. Kāne prayed and was shown the healing plants of the forest and shore; after Kānāloa was cured, the two gods shared this knowledge with humankind, establishing the practice of lāʻau lapaʻau, traditional Hawaiian herbal medicine, and ordaining the kahuna lāʻau lapaʻau who guarded the recipes — which plant for fever, which for broken bone, which for the sickness of the soul — as a sacred trust handed down within families. Illness and cure both belong to Kānāloa's watery realm — the same depths that take life also restore it. The story makes the underworld-god the founder of medicine: only the power that rules decay understands how to reverse it.

myths.title: The Octopus Reaches the Land of Kāne
myths.text: David Malo's Hawaiian Antiquities records a famous contention between the gods: the octopus — Kānāloa's kin — reaching into the islands, stretching its arms ashore and into the fresh waters that belong to Kāne. Kāne objects that the realm of land and fresh water is his; the octopus, and so Kānāloa, must keep to the sea. In the version Malo preserves, the octopus is ultimately driven back into the deep, the boundary between the brothers' domains drawn along the waterline itself. The story is told as a boundary dispute, but its subject is the frailty of every line humans draw between sea and shore — a line the tides and the heʻe's arms are always quietly redrawing. Kānāloa stays in the deep, but the deep, the myth insists, is never far.

myths.title: The Dark Realm
myths.text: Kānāloa is also lord of the underworld, the realm beneath the earth and sea where souls journey after death — a kingdom often imagined, as Beckwith notes, as a great house of coral and shell at the bottom of the sea. Unlike the Christian hell, this realm is not primarily punitive; it is the mysterious mirror of the living world, governed by the same god whose waters feed the land above. The kahuna, in the tradition recorded by Kamakau, addressed prayers to Kānāloa when illness dragged a soul toward that dark kingdom, asking the god who rules both healing and the deep to give the sick back to the sunlit world. Death, in his keeping, is less an ending than a change of address — from the island of Kāne to the house of Kānāloa.

lore.syncretism: Kānāloa is clearly related to the pan-Polynesian Tangaroa / Taʻaroa, the great sea deity of the Māori, Tahitians, and Cook Islands — the consonant correspondences (Hawaiian k- against Polynesian t-) are among the cleanest in comparative Polynesian linguistics. In Hawaiian tradition, however, he is less a creator-from-void and more a partner of Kāne, a god of depth and healing. Christian missionaries sometimes identified him with Satan because of his underworld associations, but this identification distorts a figure who was primarily beneficent. Modern Hawaiian cultural revival has reclaimed Kānāloa as a symbol of oceanic sovereignty and ecological wisdom.
lore.culturalLegacy: Kānāloa's name survives in Hawaiian place names, in the scientific names of deep-sea creatures, and in the cultural revival movements that seek to restore indigenous relationships with the ocean. He is invoked in debates over marine conservation, deep-sea mining, and the rights of native Hawaiians to their waters. The octopus, his kin, has become an emblem of intelligent, adaptable life in the Pacific.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Kānāloa is the god of what we cannot see from the surface. His realm begins where the light fails and the pressure grows. To think of him is to remember that most of the living world is ocean, and that our small islands of land are exceptions to a watery rule.

In an age of rising seas, Kānāloa is not an abstraction. He is the Pacific that is warming, acidifying, and rising around the islands that bear his name. The old stories say he sustains life; the new stories ask whether we are still worthy of that sustenance. The octopus watches from the deep, arms reaching in every direction, waiting to see what we will do.
lore.originalScriptNote: Hawaiian had no indigenous writing system before European contact. The name is written in the Latin alphabet introduced by missionaries, with macrons added by modern scholars to mark long vowels. Kānāloa is composed of ka (article or intensifier) + nā (plural or intensifier) + loa ('long, vast, far'), together evoking vastness. PUNICODEX preserves both macrons because vowel length is phonemic in Hawaiian and the feature that gives the restored name its dignity, even though the mechanical tier rule keeps the name Tier 2.
